entities.summary:
The Ruhr Uprising was a pivotal event in the aftermath of World War I, taking place in the Ruhr region of Western Germany from March 13 to April 12, 1920. This conflict was a key moment in the German Revolution, as it saw the rise of left-wing coal miners and workers who clashed with the right-wing government. The uprising was marked by violent clashes and strikes, resulting in the deaths of over 1,000 people and the destruction of property worth millions. The Ruhr Uprising had significant consequences, as it led to the eventual collapse of the right-wing government and paved the way for the establishment of the Weimar Republic.

The event was characterized by the bravery of the coal miners, who risked their lives to fight for their rights and improve working conditions. The uprising also saw the rise of influential figures such as Franz Mehring, who became a key leader of the German left-wing movement. The event's impact was felt far beyond the Ruhr region, as it contributed to the broader social and political changes taking place in Germany during this period.

One of the most lasting legacies of the Ruhr Uprising was the transformation of the German working class, which emerged from the conflict with a newfound sense of power and solidarity. As historian Franz Osterroth noted, 'The Ruhr Uprising was a turning point in the history of the German working class, marking the end of the old order and the beginning of a new era of class struggle.'
